study.title: Modulations of resting-static functional connectivity on insular by electroacupuncture in subjective tinnitus
study.study_design: Non-randomized pre-post clinical study with matched healthy control group; EG received electroacupuncture treatment, CG received no intervention
study.population: Subjective tinnitus patients treated in outpatient department of Second Department of Acupuncture and Rehabilitation of Anhui Provincial Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine, and age- and sex-matched healthy volunteers
study.inclusion_criteria: ① met the diagnostic criteria of ST; ② were between the ages of 18 and 65, right-handed; ③ suffered from subjective persistent or intermittent tinnitus, and had received no acupuncture treatment in the last 3 months; ④ were of an illness grading criteria THI second to fifth grade; ⑤ suffered no obvious abnormalities in the intracranial and ear canals by conventional MRI scan; ⑥ met the requirements of magnetic resonance examination (no metal dentures, pacemakers, stents and no claustrophobia, etc.); ⑦ volunteered to participate in this study and signed the informed consent
study.exclusion_criteria: ① possessed a history of mental or nervous system diseases; ② had a clear past record of organic diseases, such as heart, liver, kidney and hematopoietic system diseases; ③ were pregnant and lactating women; ④ might not be able to cooperate in the treatment, and could not independently complete the scale and follow-up

interventions.procedure_label_exact: electroacupuncture at SI19 (Tinggong), GB11 (Touqiaoyin), TE17 (Yifeng), GV20 (Baihui), GV15 (Yamen), GV14 (Dazhui), SJ13 (Zhongzhu)
interventions.anatomical_location_exact: acupoints on the affected side of SI19, GB11, TE17, SJ13 and the acupoints on the governor vessel of GV20, GV15, GV14
interventions.laterality_exact: acupoints on the affected side (SI19, GB11, TE17, SJ13); governor vessel (GV20, GV15, GV14)
interventions.manipulation_exact: SI19: needled with open mouth toward inner ear until ear had slight electrical shock sensation without twisting needle; GV15: needled with needle tip toward lower jaw with mouth closed, nose pinched and air blown until patient felt local pain and distension; GB11, TE17: obliquely punctured with needle tip toward ear until ear had slight electrical shock sensation; GV20, SJ13: obliquely needled until achieving de qi needling sensation (soreness, numbness, distention, heaviness, and other sensations); GV14: obliquely upward needled with needle sensation radiating around
interventions.deqi_intended_exact: yes; de qi needling sensation (a composite of sensations including soreness, numbness, distention, heaviness, and other sensations), which is believed to be an essential component of acupuncture efficacy
interventions.electrical_intensity_exact: current intensity was determined by the patient's tolerance
interventions.treatment_period_exact: 3 treatments per week, once every other day, 10 sessions total
interventions.practitioner_description_exact: performed by Professor Yang in the acupuncture department of Anhui Provincial Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine
interventions.treatment_rationale_given_exact: based on the clinical treatment experience of ST of Professor Yang Jun, the National Celebrated Traditional Chinese Medicine Expert in China, with the main treatment principle of 'Ningshen Tongqiao (Calming the mind and clearing the orifices), Tongjing Huoluo (Expediting channel and activating meridian)'; based on the possible pathogenic factors of ST 'qi and blood stagnation, spirit and auditive orifice blockage' in TCM and 'insufficient blood supply, nerve damage, immune inflammation' in modern biomedicine

interventions.procedure_label_exact: no intervention; only rs-fMRI data were collected

extraction_notes.note: No sham acupuncture or placebo control arm is present in this study. The control group (CG) consists of healthy volunteers who received no intervention. No sham procedure details are applicable.
Expectancy, credibility, and blinding were not assessed or reported in this study. The paper does not mention any such instruments.
Adverse events were not reported anywhere in the paper. No statement about presence or absence of adverse events was found.
Trial registration number was not reported in the paper.

Abstract states THI and average air conduction threshold were 'significantly lower than before (p < 0.01)', but Table 2 footnote states '*p<0.05'. Both values are preserved in extraction. This is an inconsistency within the paper.

The Z column header in Table 5 is labeled 'X' instead of 'Z' in the PDF for the MNI coordinates (apparent typographic/OCR issue in the table header). The coordinates extracted are interpreted as X, Y, Z based on the table structure and values reported.

The study design does not use randomization and there is no mention of random allocation. It is described as a clinical study where EG patients were recruited from a clinical setting and CG was publicly recruited and matched. The study_design field captures this non-randomized design.

The paper does not provide a quantitative sensory rating instrument (e.g., MASS, VAS for deqi) for the electroacupuncture sessions. De qi is mentioned only in the treatment protocol as an intended sensation goal.
The paper does not report global signal regression status in preprocessing, which may affect FC results.

The paper states in the abstract that FC results comparing EG post-treatment with CG showed decreases in INS to 'right superior frontal gyrus, left middle frontal gyrus and right anterior cuneus'; and also within-group EG post vs pre showed decreases in INS to 'right middle frontal gyrus, left superior frontal gyrus and right paracentral lobule'. These are two distinct comparisons (EG post vs CG; and EG post vs EG pre) and have been extracted as separate contrasts C2 and C3 respectively.

The correlation analysis (contrast C4) states THI score was 'negatively correlated with the reduction of FC value in INS-left superior frontal gyrus before treatment'. It is noted that 'reduction of FC value' may imply the difference between pre and post FC values, but it could also refer to the raw pre-treatment FC value relative to CG. The wording is ambiguous; the paper's exact language is preserved.

No increased FC results were reported in any contrast. All statistically significant findings were decreases (negative T-values). This may reflect analysis choices or actual data; no increases were reported.

The paper reports in abstract that 'FC of ST patients between the INS and right middle frontal gyrus, left superior frontal gyrus and right paracentral lobule showed a significant decrease after treatment' but does not clarify whether this is compared to CG or compared to pre-treatment. Based on the results section and Table 5, this corresponds to the within-group pre vs post comparison (paired t-test), which is contrast C3.
The paper does not report demographic group differences in full (e.g., education, disease duration, laterality of tinnitus, specific THI subscale scores) beyond age and gender.
